 Vs

full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 674 of 1985 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Rajbari impleading the present petitioner as defendant and opposite party Nos. 2-11 as proforma defendants praying for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land, as described in the schedule to the plaint, alleging, inter alia that the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar and was accordingly recorded in the RS khatian in the name of the said Dharani Dhar Sarkar who while in possession granted settlement of the suit land appertaining to RS khatian No. 302 and 303 on the basis of rent receipt dated 28th of Chaitra 1358 BS and 10th of Ashwin 1360 BS to one Matiur Ralunan and put him in possession on receipt of rent from him and that the said Matiur claimed title and possession in the suit land on the basis of the settlement and subsequently transferred the suit land to one Mafizuddin Mistry by a registered kabala dated 23-12-1966 and the said Mafizuddin recorded his name in Mutation Case No. 1618 of 1966-1967 and paid rent to the Government and while in possession the said Mafizuddin Mistry transferred the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 3-1-1978 and put the plaintiff in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff also mutated his name in the government Tahsil office and has been paying taxes to the government and the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land. The principal defendants have no right, title or possession in the suit land but in the last part of 1391 BS the principal defendants made a false claim as regards title to the suit land and the plaintiff on an enquiry came to learnt that the SA record of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Dharani Dhar Sarkar which has cast a cloud on the plaintiff's title and hence the suit. 

 9. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgments and all other evidence on record. The trail Court and the lower appellate Court found that admittedly the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar. The DW 1 also admitted in his evidence that the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar. The plaintiff has produced Dakhilas exhibit 4, 4 Ka and 4 Kha which was proved by PW 5 Biswanath Sen, who is a brother of scribe of the Dakhilas and this PW 5 deposed that he knows the signature of his brother and his brother wrote the Dakhilas. Both the Courts below considered this aspect of the evidence and accepted the plaintiff's case that Dharani Dhar Sarkar being the admitted owner in possession of the suit land granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Matiur Rahman. This finding of fact of the Courts below being concurrent, I do not find any reason to disagree with the said concurrent finding of fact. The submission that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents could not be substantiated by the contesting defendants by producing any evidence, mere saying that the Dakhilas are not genuine is not sufficient to prove that the Dakhilas are forged. When the defendants alleged that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents, the onus shifted on the defendants to prove the plea that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents and this onus could not be discharged by the contesting defendants. I therefore accept the concurrent finding of the Courts blow that by the Dakhilas Exhibit 4 series Matiur Rahman acquired title on the basis of settlement from admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar and that the said settlement holder transferred the suit land by a registered kabala in favour of Mafizuddin Mridha on 23-12-1966. Since the contesting defendants did not challenge the title and possession of Dharani Dhar Sarkar, I do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that there is no evidence that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was the landlord or Talukder or pattandar of the suit land inasmuch as the contesting defend-ants having admitted title of Dharani Dhar Sarkar could not raise the plea that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was not the owner of the suit land and unless the ownership of Dharani Dhar Sarkar is not disputed or challenged rather admitted by the contesting defendant such plea is not acceptable. The RS khatian shows that the suit land was recorded in the name of Dharani Dhar Sarkar. This RS khatian has not been challenged or disputed by the contesting defendants. In that view of the matter, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the plaintiff could not prove that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was the Jaminder or Talukder or pattander of the suit land is of no substance. The decision reported 35 DLR 129 has no application in the facts of the case before us. In the said decision a single Bench took the view that the plaintiff in Order to prove the settlement must prove the dakhilas by its scribe or by the executants or by the attesting witnesses. In the present case the dakhilas Exhibit 4 series have been proved by the brother of the scribe and both the Courts have accepted dakhilas as genuine documents. The contesting defendants could not produce any evidence disproving the dakhilas Exhibit 4 series and thus the said decision report in 35 DLR 129 has no application in the facts of the case. The learned Advocate has than relied on another decision reported in 43 DLR 77. In the said decision the learned Single Judge construed the provision of Order VII, rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held "The policy underlying the Order is to exclude evidence the existence of which at the date of the suit is doubtful and as to the genuine of which suspicion may arise because it was produced at the late stage. The sub-ordinate judge exercised his discretion on sound judicial principle in refusing to admit the Kabuliyat at the late stage of the suit". This is again not the case here in the present matter. Both the Court's have considered Exhibit 4 series and the evidence of PW 5 and concluded that by Exhibit 4 series the admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Matiur Rahman in 1358 and 1360 BS respectively. This Exhibit 4 series were proved by PW 5 Bishwanath Sen who is the brother of scribe of the dakhila as the scribe was then dead. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then relied on a decision in the case of Md Naimuddin Sarkar Q Naimuddin Sarkar vs Md Abdul Kalam Biswas Basiruddin Abul Kalam Azad reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237.1 have perused the said decision and it appears that the said decision relates to Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore not applicable in the present case which is one under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But then the principle enunciated in the said decision is very much applicable as it held "Plaintiff in Order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff." This proposition of law is established since long over a decade and is applicable in most of the civil litigation where the Courts are already taking the view that the plaintiff must prove his own case to get a decree and cannot rely on the weakness of the defence case. In the present case, both the Courts have concurrently held that the plaintiff has proved his case of title and possession and accordingly both the Courts have concurrently granted a decree in favour of the plaintiff. I do not, therefore, find that the decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners has any application in the facts of the case before us. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then relied on a decision in the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 32 DLR 252. In the said decision a Division Bench took the view "The records of rights of Government which is best evidence of possession at the time when such. This is a well-established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any Civil Court in an appropriate Civil suit." In the said decision their lordships also held that a Kabala executed and registered in Bangladesh in 1975 carries a presumption that the executants was a citizen of Bangladesh as no Indian national could transfer any property in Bangladesh by way of registered deed. This decision is also of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioner but it helps the learned Advocate for the opposite party as the record of right being RS khatian stands recorded in the name of the admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar and this may be treated as a piece of evidence that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was in possession of the suit land when the RS record was prepared. Both the Courts have found that the plaintiffs succeeded in proving his possession in the suit land and that the contesting defendants could not prove their possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate then relied on a decision in the case of Md Naimuddin Sardar alias Naim-uddin Sardar vs Md Abdul Kalam Biswas alias Md Abul Kalam Nasiruddin alias Abul Kalam Azad, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 3. The Appellate Division in the said decision construed the provision of section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the power of the High Court Division in interfering with a finding of fact of the Courts below. This decision is also not applicable in the facts of the case before us. The learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr A Wahab lastly relied on a decision in the case of Abdur Rahim Chowkider Abdur Rahman Sheikh since deceased vs Raji Haider, reported in 58 DLR 470. A Single Bench took the view "Finding on possession, concurrent by the Courts below being not passed on the evidence, oral and documentary and law cannot be binding in revision." The proposition of law is not disputed. The facts are distinguishable. In the present case, both the Courts have considered the evidence of PWs and have accepted the evidence of the PWs assigning cogent reason and held that the plaintiff has proved his possession in the suit land. The lower appellate Court has noticed the evidence of PW 2 and 3 who was bargadar in the suit land under Matiur Rahman for about 14 years and then under Mafizuddin for about 12 years and then PW 2 barga cultivated the suit land under the plaintiff for about 12 years. The lower appellate Court has found that this PW 2 has been in possession of the suit land for about 38 years under Matiur Rahman and then under. Mafizuddin and thereafter under the present plaintiff. This was the evidence of PW 3 also. The lower appellate Court considered the evidence of all the PWs and held concurrently with the trial Court that the plaintiff has proved his possession from the time of Dharani Dhar Sarkar. This being the position, it is not a case that the concurrent finding of facts are based on non-consideration of evidence and is permitted to be disturbed by the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. Since the finding of fact relating to title and possession is concluded by both the Courts and such findings of facts are based on consideration of the evidence, I do not find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. I do not, therefore, find any merit in this Rule.
